GUARDIANSHIP OF THE PERSON (PETITION INFORMATION SHEET)
Prepared for Morgan Lee · Riley Lee

PROPOSED GUARDIAN — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF PETITION
I, Morgan Lee, am the person proposed to serve as guardian of the person of Riley Lee, a minor born May 3, 2015. I state that my relationship to Riley Lee is: Maternal aunt. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a guardian of the person, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm Morgan Lee — or anyone else — as Riley Lee's guardian. Riley Lee's parent(s) of record, so far as known, are Jordan Alex Lee and Casey Lee, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can actually appoint a guardian of Riley Lee's person.

THIS PETITION INFORMATION SHEET DESCRIBES A COURT PROCEEDING, NOT A NOMINATION DOCUMENT
A guardianship of the person of Riley Lee under California law is established only through an actual court proceeding under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2 — a filed petition, notice, and a hearing that ends in a court order — not by a private nomination document or affidavit. California Probate Code § 1510(a) authorizes "a relative or other person on behalf of the minor, or the minor if 12 years of age or older," to file the petition that starts that proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A relative or other person on behalf of the minor, or the minor if 12 years of age or older, may file a petition for the appointment of a guardian of the minor. A relative may file a petition for the appointment of a guardian under this section regardless of the relative’s immigration status."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1510(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1510.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guardianship of a minor's person is created only through an actual court proceeding — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This document is informational: it describes the statutory guardianship-of-the-person petition process and does not itself appoint, nominate, or authorize anyone as guardian of the child named in this document. That distinction matters because a related, separately available document — a parent's own advance nomination of a guardian for their minor children, made in a will or a standalone signed writing under Probate Code §§ 1500 and 1502, or California's no-court Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit under Family Code §§ 6550–6552 — addresses a different mechanism entirely: a parent's advance designation, or a caregiver's limited authority without any court filing. This document instead addresses the separate, real court process by which a proposed guardian actually becomes a court-appointed guardian of a minor's person; it does not restate that companion document's content. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1510(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT THE PETITION MUST SAY, AND WHO MUST BE NOTIFIED
The petition to appoint a guardian of Riley Lee's person must specify the proposed guardian's name and address and Riley Lee's name and date of birth, and must state that the appointment is necessary or convenient. So far as known to the petitioner, the petition must also list the names and addresses of Riley Lee's parents and of any person who has legal custody or care of Riley Lee. At least 15 days before the hearing, notice of the hearing's time and place — together with a copy of the petition — must be served on Riley Lee personally if Riley Lee is 12 years of age or older, on any person having legal custody of Riley Lee or serving as guardian of Riley Lee's estate, on Riley Lee's parents, and on any person previously nominated as guardian for Riley Lee under Probate Code § 1500 or § 1501.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The petition shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed, shall specify the name and address of the proposed guardian and the name and date of birth of the proposed ward, and shall state that the appointment is necessary or convenient."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1510(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1510.)
  "The petition shall set forth, so far as is known to the petitioner, the names and addresses of all of the following: (1) The parents of the proposed ward. (2) The person having legal custody of the proposed ward and, if that person does not have the care of the proposed ward, the person having the care of the proposed ward."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1510(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1510.)
  "Except as provided in subdivisions (f) and (g), at least 15 days before the hearing on the petition for the appointment of a guardian, notice of the time and place of the hearing shall be given as provided in subdivisions (b), (c), (d), and (e) of this section. The notice shall be accompanied by a copy of the petition and shall include a copy of the form required by Section 68511.1 of the Government Code. The court shall not shorten the time for giving the notice of hearing under this section."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1511(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1511(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1511.)
  "Notice shall be served in the manner provided in Section 415.10 or 415.30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or in any manner authorized by the court, on all of the following persons: (1) The proposed ward if 12 years of age or older. (2) Any person having legal custody of the proposed ward, or serving as guardian of the estate of the proposed ward. (3) The parents of the proposed ward. (4) Any person nominated as a guardian for the proposed ward under Section 1500 or 1501."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1511(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1511(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1511.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the petition-content and notice requirements for a guardianship-of-the-person proceeding — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. Two of these citations (§ 1510(b) and § 1510(c)) are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1510); no additional independent source beyond § 1510 itself was found for the specific list of petition contents. The notice-recipient list is independently sourced from a separate section, § 1511, whose own two cited subsections — § 1511(a) and § 1511(b) — are likewise subsections of that single section (§ 1511); no additional independent source beyond § 1511 itself was found for that list. The statute also lets a court excuse notice to a specific person on findings this clause does not describe.

THE COURT INVESTIGATOR OR AGENCY REPORT REQUIRED BEFORE APPOINTMENT
Unless waived by the court for good cause, a court investigator, probation officer, or domestic relations investigator must investigate and file a report and recommendation on a proposed guardianship of Riley Lee's person before the court rules on the petition. If the proposed guardian is a relative, a court investigator conducts the investigation; if the proposed guardian is not a relative, the county agency designated to investigate potential dependency conducts it instead. That report must discuss, among other required topics, a social history of the proposed guardian, a social history of Riley Lee including any identified developmental, emotional, psychological, or educational needs, the relationship between Riley Lee and the proposed guardian, and the duration of the guardianship anticipated by the parents and the proposed guardian.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless waived by the court for good cause, a court investigator, probation officer, or domestic relations investigator shall make an investigation and file with the court a report and recommendation concerning each proposed guardianship of the person or guardianship of the estate. Investigations where the proposed guardian is a relative shall be made by a court investigator. Investigations where the proposed guardian is a nonrelative shall be made by the county agency designated to investigate potential dependency. The report of the investigation for a guardianship of the person shall include, but need not be limited to, a discussion of all of the following: (1) A social history of the proposed guardian. (2) A social history of the proposed ward, including, to the extent feasible, an assessment of any identified developmental, emotional, psychological, or educational needs of the proposed ward and the capability of the proposed guardian to meet those needs. (3) The relationship of the proposed ward to the proposed guardian, including the duration and character of the relationship, the circumstances under which the proposed guardian took physical custody of the proposed ward, and a statement of the proposed ward’s wishes concerning the proposed guardianship, unless the proposed ward’s developmental, physical, or emotional condition prevents the proposed ward from forming or stating their wishes concerning the proposed guardianship. (4) The duration of the guardianship anticipated by the parents and the proposed guardian and the plans of each parent and the proposed guardian to provide a stable and permanent home for the child. The court may waive this requirement when no parent is available."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1513(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1513(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1513.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real pre-appointment investigation requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1513(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. This corrects an initial research assumption in the task brief that framed the investigation requirement as arising under § 1514: on the actual statutory text, § 1513 is the investigation-and-report provision, while § 1514 instead sets out the standard the court applies in deciding whether, and whom, to appoint — covered in this document's companion clause on appointment priority. Separately, § 1513(b) describes a narrower, additional referral to the local child welfare agency when the proposed ward may be a dependent child described in Welfare and Institutions Code § 300; that narrower referral mechanism is not covered by this clause.

WHO THE COURT MAY APPOINT, AND THE ORDER OF PRIORITY
In deciding whom to appoint as guardian of Riley Lee's person, the court is governed by the same statutory chapters that govern custody decisions generally. Except in the specific circumstances addressed by Probate Code § 1510.1 or § 2105, Riley Lee's own parent may not be appointed as guardian of Riley Lee's person. Where custody is not to be granted to a parent, California Family Code § 3040(a) directs a preference first to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment, and then to any other person or persons the court deems suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In appointing a guardian of the person, the court is governed by Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 3020) and Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3040) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code, relating to custody of a minor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1514(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1514.)
  "Except as provided in Section 1510.1 or 2105, a minor’s parent may not be appointed as a guardian of the person of the minor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1514(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1514.)
  "Custody should be granted in the following order of preference according to the best interest of the child as provided in Sections 3011 and 3020: (1) To both parents jointly pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 3080) or to either parent. ... (2) If to neither parent, to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment. (3) To any other person or persons deemed by the court to be suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3040(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3040(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3040.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the appointment standard and priority order for a guardian of a minor's person — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. Two of these citations (§ 1514(b)(1) and § 1514(b)(2)) are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1514); the substantive priority order itself is independently sourced from a separate code section, Family Code § 3040(a), which § 1514(b)(1) incorporates by cross-reference for guardian-of-the-person appointments. The way § 3040(a)'s parent-preference and § 1514(b)(2)'s bar on appointing a parent as guardian of their own child's person interact — meaning the operative preferences in a guardianship-of-the-person case are actually § 3040(a)'s second and third tiers — is this clause's own synthesis of the two statutes' text, not a quotation from either.

A GUARDIANSHIP OF THE PERSON DOES NOT TERMINATE PARENTAL RIGHTS
Appointing a guardian of Riley Lee's person is a different legal act from terminating Riley Lee's parent's parental rights, and this document does not purport to do either. California Family Code § 3041(c) confirms that a finding supporting a nonparent's custody — the same detriment standard incorporated into a guardianship-of-the-person appointment — "does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents." The guardianship itself also remains subject to court termination: California Probate Code § 1601 allows the guardian, a parent, or the minor ward to petition the court to terminate the guardianship whenever termination would be in the ward's best interest, and a ward who has reached 18 years of age is entitled to have the guardianship terminated on request.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "As used in this section, “detriment to the child” includes the harm of removal from a stable placement of a child with a person who has assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of the child’s parent, fulfilling both the child’s physical needs and the child’s psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period of time. A finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3041(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3041(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3041.)
  "Upon petition of the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe, the court may make an order terminating the guardianship if the court determines that it is in the ward’s best interest to terminate the guardianship. Upon petition of a ward who is 18 years of age or older, the court shall make an order terminating the guardianship. Notice of the hearing on the petition shall be given for the period and in the manner provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 1460) of Part 1."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1601 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1601 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1601.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guardianship of a minor's person is legally distinct from, and does not itself terminate, parental rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a guardianship has no practical effect on a parent's day-to-day custody while it remains in place. These citations are two different code sections (Fam. C. § 3041(c) and Prob. C. § 1601); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Neither section addresses the separate, and more severe, formal process for terminating parental rights entirely (e.g., Family Code § 7800 et seq., governing proceedings to free a child from a parent's custody and control), which this document does not cover and which is not the same proceeding as the guardianship petition described here. An earlier research assumption treated Probate Code § 1601 as a consent-to-appointment or relative-preference statute; on the actual statutory text, § 1601 is the guardianship-termination provision quoted above, not a consent or relative-preference rule — no such standalone "relative preference" statute for guardian-of-the-person appointments was located in the Probate Code itself (the closest analog is the custody-preference order in Family Code § 3040(a), covered in this document's companion clause).

WHAT A COURT-APPOINTED GUARDIAN OF THE PERSON MAY DO ONCE APPOINTED
Once a court appoints a guardian of Riley Lee's person, California Probate Code § 2351(a) gives that guardian "the care, custody, and control of, and... charge of the education of," Riley Lee, subject to any limits the court's order states. Under § 2351(b), the court may, in its discretion, specifically limit the powers a particular guardian has, reserving certain powers or rights instead to someone else, such as the conservatee or, by analogy, to a parent whose rights the court's order does not displace.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Subject to subdivision (b), the guardian or conservator, but not a limited conservator, has the care, custody, and control of, and has charge of the education of, the ward or conservatee. This control shall not extend to personal rights retained by the conservatee, including, but not limited to, the right to receive visitors, telephone calls, and personal mail, unless specifically limited by court order."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2351(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2351(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2351.)
  "Where the court determines that it is appropriate in the circumstances of the particular conservatee, the court, in its discretion, may limit the powers and duties that the conservator would otherwise have under subdivision (a) by an order stating either of the following: (1) The specific powers that the conservator does not have with respect to the conservatee’s person and reserving the powers so specified to the conservatee. (2) The specific powers and duties the conservator has with respect to the conservatee’s person and reserving to the conservatee all other rights with respect to the conservatee’s person that the conservator otherwise would have under subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2351(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2351(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2351.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a court-appointed guardian's default powers and duties over a minor's person — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This is a single statutory section (§ 2351), citing two of its subsections (§ 2351(a) and § 2351(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. These default powers arise only from an actual court order appointing a guardian of the child's person — nothing in this document creates, limits, or confirms the care, custody, or educational authority described here, and only a signed court order following the statutory petition process can do that.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — GUARDIANSHIP PETITION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Morgan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual guardianship-of-the-person petition filed with the California probate court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not appoint a guardian; only a court order does that.]

citations.quote: As used in this section, “detriment to the child” includes the harm of removal from a stable placement of a child with a person who has assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of the child’s parent, fulfilling both the child’s physical needs and the child’s psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period of time. A finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1601 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Upon petition of the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe, the court may make an order terminating the guardianship if the court determines that it is in the ward’s best interest to terminate the guardianship. Upon petition of a ward who is 18 years of age or older, the court shall make an order terminating the guardianship. Notice of the hearing on the petition shall be given for the period and in the manner provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 1460) of Part 1.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guardianship of a minor's person is legally distinct from, and does not itself terminate, parental rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a guardianship has no practical effect on a parent's day-to-day custody while it remains in place. These citations are two different code sections (Fam. C. § 3041(c) and Prob. C. § 1601); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Neither section addresses the separate, and more severe, formal process for terminating parental rights entirely (e.g., Family Code § 7800 et seq., governing proceedings to free a child from a parent's custody and control), which this document does not cover and which is not the same proceeding as the guardianship petition described here. An earlier research assumption treated Probate Code § 1601 as a consent-to-appointment or relative-preference statute; on the actual statutory text, § 1601 is the guardianship-termination provision quoted above, not a consent or relative-preference rule — no such standalone "relative preference" statute for guardian-of-the-person appointments was located in the Probate Code itself (the closest analog is the custody-preference order in Family Code § 3040(a), covered in this document's companion clause).

expectedJSON.body: Once a court appoints a guardian of Riley Lee's person, California Probate Code § 2351(a) gives that guardian "the care, custody, and control of, and... charge of the education of," Riley Lee, subject to any limits the court's order states. Under § 2351(b), the court may, in its discretion, specifically limit the powers a particular guardian has, reserving certain powers or rights instead to someone else, such as the conservatee or, by analogy, to a parent whose rights the court's order does not displace.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2351(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (b), the guardian or conservator, but not a limited conservator, has the care, custody, and control of, and has charge of the education of, the ward or conservatee. This control shall not extend to personal rights retained by the conservatee, including, but not limited to, the right to receive visitors, telephone calls, and personal mail, unless specifically limited by court order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2351(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Where the court determines that it is appropriate in the circumstances of the particular conservatee, the court, in its discretion, may limit the powers and duties that the conservator would otherwise have under subdivision (a) by an order stating either of the following: (1) The specific powers that the conservator does not have with respect to the conservatee’s person and reserving the powers so specified to the conservatee. (2) The specific powers and duties the conservator has with respect to the conservatee’s person and reserving to the conservatee all other rights with respect to the conservatee’s person that the conservator otherwise would have under subdivision (a).

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a court-appointed guardian's default powers and duties over a minor's person — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This is a single statutory section (§ 2351), citing two of its subsections (§ 2351(a) and § 2351(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. These default powers arise only from an actual court order appointing a guardian of the child's person — nothing in this document creates, limits, or confirms the care, custody, or educational authority described here, and only a signed court order following the statutory petition process can do that.
